lesson.intro: Many interview questions ask about the best contiguous stretch: the longest substring without repeats, the shortest subarray reaching a sum. A sliding window answers them in one pass. Learn one template for fixed and variable windows and the classic problems that use it.
objectives: Recognize contiguous-range problems a window can solve
Write fixed and variable windows from one template
Maintain window state with sums, sets and count maps
Explain why a while inside a for is still O(n)

sections.title: From brute force to a window
sections.key: A sliding window keeps a running summary of a contiguous range and updates it as the range moves: add what enters, remove what leaves, O(n) in total.
sections.body:
You want the best average temperature over any 3 consecutive hours. Recomputing each window from scratch is O(n k), yet neighbors overlap: one reading leaves, one arrives, k - 1 are shared.

[[visual]]

Signals:

- **Contiguous** subarray or substring. A subsequence, whose items need not be adjacent, is not a window.
- Longest, shortest, maximum, minimum or count over such ranges.
- A condition: "at most k distinct", "no repeats", "sum at least target".

A window is **fixed size** (k is given) or **variable size** (it grows right and shrinks left to keep a rule true). Both pointers only move forward, so the work is linear.

A variable window over sums needs a **monotonic** rule: with positive numbers, growing raises the sum and shrinking lowers it. Negative numbers break that; use prefix sums with a hash map instead.

visual.title: Windows of k = 3 over [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
visual.caption: Each slide subtracts the item leaving on the left and adds the item entering on the right: O(1) per step.

sections.tip: The word "contiguous" (or "substring", or "consecutive") in a problem is the strongest single hint that a sliding window applies.

check.question: Which problem is NOT a good fit for a sliding window?
choices: The longest substring with at most 2 distinct characters
The longest increasing subsequence, where the chosen items need not be adjacent
The maximum sum of any 5 consecutive values
The shortest subarray of positive numbers with sum at least 50
check.explanation: A window always covers a contiguous range. A subsequence can skip items, so there is no single range to slide; that problem is solved with dynamic programming. The other three are contiguous-range problems.

sections.title: Fixed-size windows
sections.key: Build the first window of k items, then slide: add `nums[right]`, remove `nums[right - k]`, update the answer. Start a maximum from the first window, never 0.
sections.body:
With fixed size k: sum the first k items, then for each `right` from k to n - 1 add `nums[right]`, remove `nums[right - k]` (the item that fell out) and update the answer.

An array of n items has n - k + 1 windows. For `[2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]` and k = 3 the sums are 8, 7, 9 and 6, so the best is 9, the window [5, 1, 3]. O(n) time, O(1) space.

[[visual]]

Fixed windows work with negative numbers too, because the rule does not choose the size. So start a maximum from the first window's sum: with all-negative input, 0 is no real window sum.

A set as the state answers "does any window of size k hold a duplicate?": add the new item, remove the one that leaves.

visual.title: Two equivalent loops

items.title: Single loop
points: Record once the window is full: `right >= k - 1`

visual.caption: Pick one form and stick with it: mixing them causes off-by-one bugs.

sections.code:
def window_averages(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])                # build the first window
    result = [window / k]
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[right]             # item entering on the right
        window -= nums[right - k]         # item leaving on the left
        result.append(window / k)
    return result

def has_duplicate_within_k(nums, k):
    seen = set()
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
        if right >= k - 1:                # full: drop the oldest item
            seen.remove(nums[right - k + 1])
    return False

print(window_averages([1, 3, 2, 6, -1, 4, 1, 8, 2], 5))
# [2.2, 2.8, 2.4, 3.6, 2.8]
print(has_duplicate_within_k([1, 2, 1, 3], 3))   # True
sections.deeper:
**Anagram windows.** A count map of the window's letters, compared with the pattern's counts, finds every window of length k that is an anagram of the pattern.

**Window maximum.** The largest value in every window needs more than one running variable: when the maximum leaves, you cannot recover the next one. A monotonic deque solves it in O(n), covered in the stacks and queues pack.
sections.pitfall: Starting `best = 0` when looking for a maximum. If every number is negative, no window sums to 0, but the function returns 0 anyway. Initialize from the first window.

activity.title: Slide a fixed window
activity.prompt: Run it and check each window sum against a quick mental add. The code compares sums with threshold * k so it never divides. Then change k as the task says and predict every line first.

props.code:
nums = [2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5, 8]
k = 3
threshold = 4      # count windows whose average is at least this

window = sum(nums[:k])
count = 1 if window >= threshold * k else 0
print(f"window 0..{k - 1}: sum {window}")
for right in range(k, len(nums)):
    window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
    if window >= threshold * k:
        count += 1
    print(f"window {right - k + 1}..{right}: sum {window}")
print("windows with average >= threshold:", count)
props.task: Change k to 4. Predict each window sum and the final count before you run it.
props.expectOutput:
window 0..3: sum 8
window 1..4: sum 11
window 2..5: sum 14
window 3..6: sum 17
window 4..7: sum 23
windows with average >= threshold: 2

check.question: What is the maximum sum of 2 consecutive items in [4, -1, 3, 5, -2]?
check.explanation: The windows are [4, -1] = 3, [-1, 3] = 2, [3, 5] = 8 and [5, -2] = 3, so the best is 8. 9 would need the non-adjacent 4 and 5.

sections.title: Variable-size windows: grow and shrink
sections.key: Grow the window on the right; shrink from the left while it is invalid (longest problems) or while it is valid (shortest problems), recording in the right place.
sections.body:
"Find the shortest subarray of positive numbers with sum at least 7." The size is not given, so let the window breathe: grow it on the right, shrink it from the left, and record answers along the way.

[[visual]]

- **Longest valid window:** shrink while invalid, then record after the loop, when the window is valid again.
- **Shortest valid window:** shrink while valid, recording inside the loop, because each shrink step is a smaller valid window.

[[visual 2]]

The `while` inside the `for` looks quadratic, but `left` only moves forward, at most n times in total. Each element enters once and leaves at most once: O(n). Give this **amortized** argument when an interviewer asks about the nested loop.

steps.label: Move right one step and add nums[right] to the window state
While invalid (longest) or valid (shortest): shrink
steps.detail: Shortest: record right - left + 1 first. Then remove nums[left] and move left forward

steps.label: Longest: record right - left + 1
steps.detail: The window is valid again here

sections.code:
def min_subarray_len(target, nums):    # positive numbers only
    left, window = 0, 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        window += x
        while window >= target:            # valid: record, then shrink
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            window -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

print(min_subarray_len(7, [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]))   # 2
print(min_subarray_len(100, [1, 2, 3]))          # 0
sections.pitfall: Shrinking with `if` instead of `while`. One removal may not restore the rule, and for shortest problems you skip smaller valid windows that a few more removals would have found.

check.question: In a "longest valid window" problem, where do you update the answer?
choices: Inside the shrink loop, before removing nums[left]
Only when right reaches the end of the array
Before adding nums[right] to the window
After the shrink loop, when the window is valid again
check.explanation: For longest problems you shrink while the window is invalid, so right after the loop it is valid, and that is the moment to measure it. Recording inside the loop would measure invalid windows. Recording inside the loop is correct for shortest problems.

sections.title: Windows with a hash map: counting what is inside
sections.key: When the rule is about the characters inside a window, keep a count map: add on the right, decrement on the left, and delete keys that reach zero.
sections.body:
No repeats, at most k distinct, contains every letter of a pattern: the window state becomes a map of counts.

**At most k distinct:** add `s[right]`; while `len(counts) > k`, decrement `counts[s[left]]`, delete the key at zero, and move left. Then record. Deleting zero counts matters, because `len(counts)` is how you measure distinct characters.

**Longest substring without repeats** uses the rule "no count above 1":

[[visual]]

**Last-index variant:** store where each character was last seen and jump `left` straight past it. That index may be older than the window, so write `left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)`. Without `max`, `"abba"` moves left backward at the final a and reports 3, not 2.

Both run in O(n). Space is O(m) for m distinct characters, bounded by the alphabet: O(1) for 26 lowercase letters.
sections.code:
def longest_with_k_distinct(s, k):
    counts, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
        while len(counts) > k:                # too many distinct: shrink
            out = s[left]
            counts[out] -= 1
            if counts[out] == 0:
                del counts[out]               # keep len(counts) honest
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)    # window is valid here
    return best

print(longest_with_k_distinct("eceba", 2))     # 3  ("ece")
print(longest_with_k_distinct("aabbcc", 1))    # 2
sections.pitfall: Decrementing a count to zero without deleting the key. The map still lists that character, so `len(counts)` overstates the distinct characters and the window shrinks more than it should.

activity.title: Longest substring without repeats
activity.prompt: Adapt the count-map window from this section: the rule is that no character appears twice. Then try the last-index version and make sure "abba" returns 2.

check.question: With a last-index map, why write left = max(left, last[ch] + 1) instead of left = last[ch] + 1?
choices: To avoid an off-by-one in the window length
Because max is faster than an if statement
The stored index may be from before the current window, and without max, left could move backward
So that left never equals right
check.explanation: A character's last index can lie to the left of the window. Jumping to it would move left backward and pull already-excluded repeats back in, as "abba" shows. max keeps left moving forward only.

sections.title: Longest repeating character replacement
sections.key: A window becomes one repeated letter with `length - max count` replacements, so it is valid when that is at most k: then it is a standard longest window.
sections.body:
Given a string of uppercase letters and k, you may replace up to k characters. How long is the longest substring you can turn into one repeated letter?

For one window, keep its most frequent letter and replace everything else. It needs `length - max count` replacements, so it is valid when **length - max count <= k**. Now it is a standard longest window: grow, update the counts, shrink while invalid, record after.

[[visual]]

Recomputing the max count over 26 letters costs O(26) per step, so the scan is O(26 n), which is O(n).

visual.title: "AABABBA" with k = 1
visual.caption: Needed = length - max count. Answer: 4, for example AABA becomes AAAA.

sections.deeper: **A well-known optimization** keeps `max_count` as the largest count ever seen and never decreases it, and shrinks by a single step instead of a loop. The window then never gets shorter than the best length so far: it slides, and it grows only when some letter's count beats the old maximum. It is correct but subtle. In an interview the clear version is enough unless you are asked for more.
sections.pitfall: Counting over the whole string instead of the window, or forgetting to decrement the letter that leaves on the left. The rule is about `s[left..right]`, so the counts must describe exactly that window.

check.question: A window is "ABBBC" and k = 1. How many replacements does it need, and is it valid?
choices: 1 replacement, so it is valid
3 replacements, so it is invalid
2 replacements, so it is invalid
0 replacements, because B already repeats
check.explanation: The length is 5 and the most frequent letter, B, appears 3 times, so 5 - 3 = 2 characters (A and C) must change. That is more than k = 1, so the window must shrink.

sections.title: Buy and sell stock: a window that remembers the minimum
sections.key: For each sell day the best buy day is the cheapest day before it, so keep the lowest price so far and track the best `price - lowest`.
sections.body:
Prices by day are `[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]`. You buy on one day and sell on a later day: what is the maximum profit? Checking every pair is O(n^2).

Picture a window from the buy day (`left`) to the sell day (`right`). As `right` moves, `left` only jumps when a new lowest price appears. The whole window state is the lowest price so far.

[[visual]]

If prices only fall, every profit is at most 0, so the answer is 0. `max(prices) - min(prices)` fails, because the maximum may come before the minimum: selling before buying.

O(n) time, O(1) space. The same running summary solves other "best pair with i < j" problems, such as the largest temperature rise.

visual.title: Stock prices by day
visual.caption: Best: 5, buying at 1 on day 1 and selling at 6 on day 4.

sections.deeper:
**Order inside the loop.** Either order works: compute today's profit with the lowest price from earlier days, or update the lowest price first, which only adds a harmless profit of 0 for buying and selling on the same day.

**Greedy, DP or window?** All three views are right. The best answer ending today depends only on a summary of the past, the minimum, which is exactly a window whose left edge only moves forward.
sections.pitfall: Computing `max(prices) - min(prices)`. The maximum can come before the minimum, which means selling before buying: for `[5, 1]` it reports 4 when the real answer is 0.

check.question: With prices [3, 8, 1, 4], what is the maximum profit from one buy followed by one later sell?
check.explanation: Buying at 3 and selling at 8 gives 5. Buying at 1 and selling at 4 gives only 3. 7 would mean buying at 1 and selling at 8, but 8 comes before 1.

sections.title: Practice: choosing and debugging windows
sections.key: Ask four questions: is it contiguous, fixed or variable, what state adds and removes one item in O(1), and is the validity rule monotonic?
sections.body:
Before coding a window, answer four questions out loud:

- **Contiguous?** If the answer may skip elements, it is not a window.
- **Fixed or variable?** k given: fixed. Longest or shortest range meeting a rule: variable.
- **What state?** A sum, count map, set or lowest price. A running maximum cannot drop the item that leaves; a monotonic deque keeps the candidates instead.
- **Is the rule monotonic?** Shrinking a valid window must keep it valid. Positive sums, "at most k distinct" and "no repeats" qualify; sums with negatives do not.

[[visual]]

Common bugs: `if` instead of `while` when shrinking; recording in the wrong place; not deleting zero counts; length as `right - left` instead of `right - left + 1`; a maximum started at 0; a variable window on sums with negatives.

visual.title: Window cheat sheet
rows: Max sum of k consecutive items
Shrink while a count > 1, record after
Longest with at most k distinct
Record and shrink while sum >= target
Shrink while length - max count > k
Best time to buy and sell stock

activity.title: Longest repeating character replacement
activity.prompt: Use the rule from the trace table: the window is valid when length - max count <= k. Shrink while invalid and record after the loop. Check that "AABABBA" with k = 1 gives 4 before you submit.

check.question: Your longest-window solution returns 2 for "abc" under the rule "no repeated characters". Which bug is most likely?
choices: The window length is computed as right - left instead of right - left + 1
The shrink step uses while instead of if
The counts map deletes keys that reach zero
left starts at 0
check.explanation: The window 0..2 holds 3 characters, but right - left gives 2. Indexes are inclusive at both ends, so the length is right - left + 1. Using while and deleting zero counts are both correct.

keyTerms.definition: A technique that keeps a summary of a contiguous range and updates it as the range moves, instead of recomputing it.
A window of given length k that slides one step at a time, adding the entering item and removing nums[right - k].
A window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left to find the longest or shortest range meeting a rule.
What you track about the window, such as a sum, a set or a count map, updated in O(1) per item.
The condition a window must meet, such as no repeated characters or sum at least target.
A rule where shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (and growing an invalid one keeps it invalid), which variable windows require.
Total linear work even with a nested loop, because each element enters and leaves the window at most once.
A map from each character to the index where it last appeared, letting left jump past a repeat in one step.

summary: A window updates a summary of a contiguous range, turning O(n k) or O(n^2) into O(n).
Fixed windows add `nums[right]` and remove `nums[right - k]`; start a maximum from the first window.
Variable windows: shrink while invalid for longest, while valid for shortest.
Delete zero counts so the number of keys stays accurate.
Each pointer only moves forward, so the nested loop is O(n).
Sum windows need positive numbers; with negatives, use prefix sums and a hash map.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a sliding window finds the longest stretch of a playlist with no repeated song, why the left edge only ever moves forward, and why that makes the whole scan linear.

questions.question: What must be true about the answer for a sliding window to apply?
choices: It is a contiguous subarray or substring
It comes from a sorted input
It contains no duplicate values
It can be any subset of the items
questions.explanation: A window always covers consecutive items. Sorting is not required (and would destroy the order that defines the ranges), duplicates are fine, and arbitrary subsets are not windows.

questions.question: Which problems can a sliding window solve directly? Select all that apply.
choices: Maximum sum of any 4 consecutive values
Longest substring with no repeated characters
Longest increasing subsequence
Shortest subarray of positive numbers with sum at least S
Number of pairs (i, j) anywhere in the array with nums[i] + nums[j] = k
questions.explanation: The first, second and fourth ask about contiguous ranges with a monotonic rule. A subsequence can skip items, and arbitrary pairs are not ranges at all; those need dynamic programming and a hash map respectively.

questions.question: A brute force recomputes the sum of every window of size k from scratch in an array of n items. What is its time complexity in Big-O notation?
questions.explanation: There are about n windows and each costs k additions, so O(n k). Sliding the window reuses the shared k - 1 items and brings it to O(n).

questions.question: Why does a variable window fail for "shortest subarray with sum at least S" when the array contains negative numbers?
choices: Negative numbers cannot be stored in a running sum
Shrinking no longer reliably lowers the sum, so you cannot tell which pointer to move
The window would need to move backward, which Python does not allow
No algorithm can solve the problem with negative numbers
questions.explanation: With negatives, removing an item from the left can raise the sum, and adding one can lower it, so a too-small window might become valid by shrinking. The rule is no longer monotonic. Prefix sums with a sorted structure or a deque solve that version.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the fixed window removes the item that leaves on the left.
questions.code:
def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[right] - _____
        best = max(best, window)
    return best
choices: nums[right - k + 1]
nums[right - 1]
nums[k]
nums[right - k]
questions.explanation: Before this step the window was right - k to right - 1. Adding nums[right] and dropping nums[right - k] keeps exactly k items. nums[right - k + 1] is still inside the new window.

questions.question: How many windows of size k = 3 does an array of 10 items have?
questions.explanation: Windows start at indexes 0 through n - k = 7, so there are n - k + 1 = 8 of them.

questions.question: max_sum_k([-3, -1, -4, -2], 2) prints 0, but the best window sum is -4. What is the bug?
choices: The window should subtract nums[right - k + 1]
right >= k - 1 should be right >= k
best starts at 0, which no window reaches when every number is negative
window should start at nums[0]
questions.explanation: The window sums are -4, -5 and -6, all below 0, so max never replaces the starting 0. Start best at float("-inf") or at the first full window's sum. The sliding logic itself is correct.

questions.question: In the single-loop fixed window, which adds nums[right] on every step, when is the window first full?
choices: When right == k
When right == 0
When right == k - 1
When right == len(nums) - k
questions.explanation: Indexes 0 through k - 1 are k items, so the window is full once right reaches k - 1. From then on you record an answer each step, and from right == k you also remove nums[right - k].

questions.question: Which window state answers "does any window of size k contain a duplicate?" in O(n)?
choices: A running sum of the window
A sorted copy of each window
A stack of the window's items
A set of the window's items, adding the new item and removing the one that leaves
questions.explanation: A set gives O(1) membership checks for the new item, and removing the item that slides out keeps it equal to the window. A sum cannot detect duplicates, and sorting each window costs O(k log k) per step.

questions.question: Put the steps of the shortest-valid-window loop in order (for example, shortest subarray with sum at least target).
items: Add nums[right] to the window sum
While the sum is at least the target, record right - left + 1
Still inside that loop, subtract nums[left] and move left forward
Move right to the next index and repeat
questions.explanation: Grow first, then record and shrink as long as the window stays valid, because every successful shrink is a shorter valid window. Then grow again.

questions.question: What does min_subarray_len(11, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) return (shortest subarray with sum at least 11)?
questions.explanation: [3, 4, 5] sums to 12 and has length 3. No two consecutive items reach 11 (the biggest pair, 4 + 5, is 9).

questions.question: min_subarray_len(7, [1, 1, 1, 7]) returns 4, but [7] alone has length 1. What is wrong?
questions.code:
def min_subarray_len(target, nums):
    left = 0
    window = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        window += x
        if window >= target:
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            window -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best
choices: It shrinks with if, so only one item leaves per step and the shorter valid windows are never measured
The length should be right - left
best should start at 0
window -= nums[left] must come after left += 1
questions.explanation: When 7 arrives, the window 0..3 is valid and recorded, then one item leaves and the loop moves on, although 1..3 and 2..3 and 3..3 are all still valid. A while loop keeps shrinking and records each of them, reaching length 1.

questions.question: Why is the variable window O(n) even though a while loop sits inside the for loop?
choices: The while loop runs at most once per iteration
left only moves forward, at most n times in total, so each element is added once and removed at most once
The while loop only runs when the window is valid, which is rare
Python merges nested loops into a single loop
questions.explanation: Count total work, not per-iteration work. right makes n steps and left makes at most n steps over the whole run, so all the inner iterations together cost O(n). A single iteration of the while loop can run many times, which is why the first choice is wrong.

questions.question: In a "shortest valid window" problem, where is the answer recorded?
choices: Inside the shrink loop, while the window is still valid
After the shrink loop
Only at the very end
Before adding nums[right]
questions.explanation: You shrink while the window is valid, so each pass through the loop body sees a valid window that is shorter than the last; record it before removing nums[left]. After the loop the window is invalid.

questions.question: State the variable sliding window template in words.
questions.answer: Move right forward and add the new item to the window state. While the window breaks the rule (for longest) or satisfies it (for shortest), update the answer if needed, remove the left item and move left forward. For longest problems, record the window length after the shrink loop.
questions.explanation: Being able to say this template is what lets you write any window problem quickly: only the state, the rule and the recording spot change.

questions.question: Fill the blank in the shrink loop of the at-most-k-distinct window.
choices: counts[out] = 1
del counts[out]
left -= 1
break
questions.explanation: A character with count 0 is no longer in the window, so its key must go, or len(counts) keeps counting it as distinct and the loop shrinks too far.

questions.question: What is the length of the longest substring without repeating characters in "pwwkew"?
questions.explanation: "wke" has three distinct characters. "pwke" is not a substring, because the characters are not contiguous.

questions.question: longest_unique("abba") returns 3, but the answer is 2. What is the bug?
choices: last[ch] should be stored before the check
The length should be right - left
left can move backward when the stored index is outside the window; use left = max(left, last[ch] + 1)
best should only be updated when ch is new
questions.explanation: At the second b, left jumps to 2. At the final a, last["a"] is 0, so left drops back to 1 and the window "bba" (with a repeat) is measured as 3. Taking the max keeps left from moving backward.

questions.question: What does longest_with_k_distinct("eceba", 2) return?
questions.explanation: "ece" uses two distinct letters and has length 3. Adding b makes three distinct letters, so the window shrinks to "eb", and nothing longer appears later.

questions.question: How much extra space does a count-map window use on a string of lowercase English letters?
choices: O(n) in every case
O(1): at most 26 keys
O(k^2), where k is the window length
questions.explanation: The map holds one key per distinct character in the window, which can never exceed the 26-letter alphabet, so the space is bounded by a constant. For an unbounded alphabet you would say O(min(n, alphabet size)).

questions.question: How many replacements does the window "AABBB" need to become a single repeated letter?
questions.explanation: Length 5 minus the most frequent letter's count (B appears 3 times) is 2: replace the two As.

questions.question: For longest repeating character replacement, what is the answer for "AABABBA" with k = 2?
questions.explanation: "AABAB" (or "BABBA") has length 5 with a most frequent letter appearing 3 times, so 2 replacements suffice. Any length-6 window has 3 As and 3 Bs and needs 3 replacements.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the window shrinks while it needs more than k replacements.
questions.code:
counts[s[right]] = counts.get(s[right], 0) + 1
while _____:
    counts[s[left]] -= 1
    left += 1
best = max(best, right - left + 1)
choices: max(counts.values()) > k
(right - left + 1) - max(counts.values()) > k
right - left + 1 > k
len(counts) > k
questions.explanation: Replacements needed = window length - count of its most common letter, and the window is invalid when that exceeds k. len(counts) > k is the at-most-k-distinct rule, a different problem.

questions.question: Why is "window length minus the count of its most frequent letter" the number of replacements a window needs?
questions.answer: To turn the window into one repeated letter with the fewest changes, keep the letter that already appears most often and replace every other character. Those other characters number length minus the max count.
questions.explanation: Choosing any other target letter keeps fewer characters, so it needs more replacements. This turns a scary-sounding problem into a standard longest-window rule.

questions.question: What is the maximum profit for prices [7, 6, 4, 3, 1] with one buy followed by one later sell (0 if no profit is possible)?
questions.explanation: Prices only fall, so every later price is lower than any earlier one and every trade loses money. The answer is 0: do not trade.

questions.question: max_profit([9, 2, 6]) returns 7, but the best trade (buy at 2, sell at 6) makes 4. What is wrong?
choices: max and min are O(n^2) together
It should return min(prices) - max(prices)
It ignores the last price
It pairs the earlier high (9) with the later low (2), which means selling before buying
questions.explanation: The order of days matters: you can only sell after you buy. Track the lowest price so far and, for each day, the profit from selling today; that respects the order in one O(n) pass.

questions.question: Fill the blank to complete the one-pass stock profit solution.
questions.code:
def max_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, _____)
    return best
choices: lowest - p
p - prices[0]
p - lowest
best - lowest
questions.explanation: Selling today at p after buying at the lowest earlier (or same-day) price earns p - lowest. Updating lowest first only adds a same-day profit of 0, which is harmless. p - prices[0] fixes the buy day to day 0.

questions.question: What state does the best-time-to-buy-and-sell solution keep as it scans the prices?
choices: A count of each price
The lowest price seen so far
The sum of all prices so far
A sorted list of earlier prices
questions.explanation: For each sell day, the best buy is the cheapest earlier day, so the lowest price so far is the only summary of the past you need. It gives O(1) space.

questions.question: Match each problem with the right technique.

pairs.left: Max sum of k consecutive items
pairs.right: Fixed window with a running sum
Variable window with counts or last index

pairs.left: Shortest subarray with sum >= S, positive numbers
pairs.right: Variable window with a running sum

pairs.left: Best time to buy and sell stock
Count subarrays with sum k, negatives allowed
pairs.right: Prefix sums with a hash map

questions.explanation: The last one is the trap: negative numbers break the monotonic rule a variable window needs, so you count earlier prefix sums equal to prefix - k instead.

questions.question: You need the maximum value in every window of size k. Why is one running variable not enough, and what is used instead?
choices: When the maximum leaves the window, one number cannot tell you the next maximum; a monotonic deque keeps the candidates in order
Maximums can be negative, so you should keep a running sum instead
A running maximum works if you reset it every k steps
A count map finds the maximum in O(1)
questions.explanation: Removing an item from a sum is just a subtraction, but removing the current maximum leaves you no record of the runner-up. A deque of indexes with decreasing values keeps every possible future maximum and gives O(n) overall.

questions.question: Which of these are common sliding window bugs? Select all that apply.
choices: Shrinking with if instead of while
Writing the window length as right - left
Forgetting to delete keys whose count reaches zero
Moving left only forward
Starting a maximum at 0 when values can be negative
questions.explanation: Moving left only forward is correct; it is what makes windows O(n). The other four are the bugs interviewers see most often.
